metadata.description: Deploys a standalone VNet with a Private Link Service, Standard internal load balancer, and a Flexible-orchestration virtual machine scale set of Linux forwarding appliances for Fabric or Azure Data Factory managed private endpoint connectivity.
metadata.cloudInitSource: cloud-init/forwarder.yaml is the source of truth for the cloudInitTemplate variable. Run tools/Build-Template.ps1 after editing it, and tools/Build-Template.ps1 -Verify to confirm this file is in sync.

metadata.description: Lowercase prefix used in resource names.

Subnet holding the scale set. Scale set instances take dynamic addresses, so the target's firewall must allow this whole prefix. Keep it small: a /27 leaves 27 usable addresses and keeps the on-premises firewall change request narrow.
Private IPv4 address of the target SQL Server reached through hub/spoke or hybrid connectivity.
SSH public key for the forwarding instances. No public IP is created.
Optional private CIDR allowed to reach SSH on the forwarding instances. Leave empty to create no SSH rule at all.
Instance size. D-series supports accelerated networking, which B-series does not; the appliance is packet-forwarding bound, so the NIC path matters far more than vCPU count.
Number of forwarding instances. Autoscale is deliberately not configured: scale-in kills in-flight TCP sessions because Azure Load Balancer does not drain connections.
Zones to spread instances across. Use an empty array in regions without availability zones.
Requires a VM size that supports it. Set false if vmSize is changed to a size without accelerated networking support.

Creates a NAT gateway for outbound internet from the forwarder subnet. Not required for the data path, for this template's cloud-init, or for extension installation, because a supported Azure Linux Agent downloads extension packages through the fabric controller on 168.63.129.16. Enable it only to allow in-guest OS patching or to install extra packages.
Replaces instances the Application Health extension reports unhealthy.
Loopback port for the health endpoint the Application Health extension probes. Never exposed to the VNet, so it needs no NSG rule.
Must be a generation 2 image because the instances use trusted launch.
Subscriptions allowed to discover this Private Link Service. Add the subscription containing the Fabric or ADF managed VNet.
Consumer subscriptions whose private endpoint requests are approved automatically. Use an empty array to require manual approval.

properties.description: Traffic arriving from the Private Link Service NAT subnet.
Health probes from 168.63.129.16. DNAT'd to the target like real traffic, so this tests the whole path, not liveness.
Explicit floor so an added rule must be deliberate.
Optional administrative access from a private network.

variables.cloudInitTemplate:
#cloud-config
# Private Link forwarding appliance — VMSS instance bootstrap.
#
# This file is the single source of truth for instance configuration. `tools/Build-Template.ps1`
# embeds it into the `cloudInitTemplate` variable in azuredeploy.json and ARM substitutes the two
# placeholders below at deploy time, so the template stays self-contained and portal-deployable
# while this file remains reviewable as real YAML. Run the build script after editing; deploy.ps1
# refuses to deploy a template whose embedded copy has drifted from this file.
#
#   __FORWARD_MAP__   newline-separated "listenPort targetHost targetPort" records
#   __HEALTH_PORT__   loopback TCP port serving the health endpoint for the Application Health extension
#
# Two constraints shape everything here:
#
#   1. No package installation. iptables, systemd and bash all ship in the Azure Ubuntu
#      marketplace image. VMSS instances in Flexible orchestration have no default outbound
#      internet access, and platform default outbound access retired in September 2025, so a
#      cloud-init that runs `apt install` hangs for the whole boot in a locked-down subnet.
#      Everything below works with zero egress.
#
#   2. Convergence, not first-boot setup. iptables rules live in the kernel and are lost on
#      every reboot. Nothing here writes rules once; a systemd unit rebuilds them at boot and a
#      timer reconciles drift, so reboot, platform patching, reimage and scale-out all land on
#      identical state.

package_update: false
package_upgrade: false

write_files:
  # nf_conntrack must be resident before systemd-sysctl applies the tunables below, otherwise
  # net.netfilter.* keys do not exist yet and are silently skipped at early boot.
  - path: /etc/modules-load.d/private-link-forwarder.conf
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      nf_conntrack

  - path: /etc/sysctl.d/99-private-link-forwarder.conf
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      # The Azure NIC has enableIPForwarding=true; this is the matching guest-side half.
      # Both are required — either one alone silently blackholes forwarded traffic.
      net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1

      # Loose reverse-path filtering. Return traffic from on-premises can arrive on a path the
      # strict check does not consider symmetric once a hub firewall or UDR is inserted.
      net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 2
      net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 2

      # MASQUERADE burns one source port per concurrent flow toward the same target tuple.
      # Spark with a high JDBC numPartitions opens many parallel connections, so the ephemeral
      # range and the conntrack ceiling are the real scale limits on this appliance — not CPU.
      net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 10000 65000
      net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 262144

      # Detect a dead peer well inside the Private Link service's ~5 minute idle timeout so
      # conntrack entries for reset flows are reclaimed promptly.
      net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time = 120
      net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl = 30
      net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes = 4

  - path: /etc/private-link-forwarder/forward.map
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      # listenPort targetHost targetPort
      __FORWARD_MAP__

  - path: /usr/local/sbin/private-link-forwarder
    permissions: '0755'
    content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # Builds the DNAT/SNAT/forward rules for the Private Link forwarding appliance.
      #
      # All rules live in dedicated PLS_FORWARDER chains rather than in the built-in chains.
      # That makes `apply` a full rebuild that is idempotent and atomic enough to re-run at any
      # time, and makes `flush` able to remove everything this appliance owns without disturbing
      # rules added by any other agent on the host.
      set -euo pipefail

      CHAIN=PLS_FORWARDER
      MAP=/etc/private-link-forwarder/forward.map

      # Derive the uplink instead of hardcoding eth0. Accelerated networking on D-series adds a
      # bound VF interface, and a second NIC would shift the name — a wrong -i match here fails
      # open as "no forwarding at all", which is the hardest symptom to diagnose.
      uplink() {
        local dev=''
        dev="$( (ip -4 route show default 2>/dev/null || true) | awk '{print $5; exit}' )" || true
        printf '%s' "${dev:-eth0}"
      }

      # Emit each mapping as "listenPort targetHost targetPort", skipping comments and blanks.
      mappings() {
        [ -r "$MAP" ] || return 0
        while read -r listen host port _rest; do
          case "${listen:-}" in ''|\#*) continue ;; esac
          [ -n "${host:-}" ] && [ -n "${port:-}" ] || continue
          printf '%s %s %s\n' "$listen" "$host" "$port"
        done < "$MAP"
      }

      ensure_chain() {
        local table="$1" parent="$2"
        iptables -t "$table" -N "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null || iptables -t "$table" -F "$CHAIN"
        iptables -t "$table" -C "$parent" -j "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null \
          || iptables -t "$table" -I "$parent" 1 -j "$CHAIN"
      }

      apply() {
        local dev
        dev="$(uplink)"

        ensure_chain nat PREROUTING
        ensure_chain nat POSTROUTING
        ensure_chain filter FORWARD

        while read -r listen host port; do
          # Inbound from the load balancer: rewrite the destination to the real target.
          iptables -t nat -A "$CHAIN" -i "$dev" -p tcp --dport "$listen" \
            -j DNAT --to-destination "$host:$port"
          # Outbound to the target: rewrite the source to this instance, so the target needs a
          # return route only to this VNet rather than to the Fabric managed VNet.
          iptables -t nat -A "$CHAIN" -p tcp -d "$host" --dport "$port" -j MASQUERADE
          iptables -A "$CHAIN" -p tcp -d "$host" --dport "$port" -j ACCEPT
        done < <(mappings)

        # Return traffic for every mapping, in one rule rather than one per target.
        iptables -A "$CHAIN" -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
      }

      flush() {
        local pair table parent
        for pair in nat:PREROUTING nat:POSTROUTING filter:FORWARD; do
          table="${pair%%:*}"
          parent="${pair##*:}"
          # Loop: a repeated apply/upgrade could have left more than one jump in place.
          while iptables -t "$table" -C "$parent" -j "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null; do
            iptables -t "$table" -D "$parent" -j "$CHAIN"
          done
        done
        for table in nat filter; do
          iptables -t "$table" -F "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null || true
          iptables -t "$table" -X "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null || true
        done
      }

      # Exit 0 only when every rule this appliance owns is present. Used by the reconcile timer
      # and by the health endpoint, so it must be cheap and must never mutate state.
      verify() {
        local dev found=0
        dev="$(uplink)"

        iptables -t nat -C PREROUTING -j "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null || return 1
        iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -j "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null || return 1
        iptables -C FORWARD -j "$CHAIN" 2>/dev/null || return 1

        while read -r listen host port; do
          found=1
          iptables -t nat -C "$CHAIN" -i "$dev" -p tcp --dport "$listen" \
            -j DNAT --to-destination "$host:$port" 2>/dev/null || return 1
          iptables -t nat -C "$CHAIN" -p tcp -d "$host" --dport "$port" -j MASQUERADE 2>/dev/null || return 1
        done < <(mappings)

        # An empty map means the appliance is unconfigured, which is a failure, not a pass.
        [ "$found" -eq 1 ] || return 1
        [ "$(cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward)" = "1" ] || return 1
        return 0
      }

      case "${1:-apply}" in
        apply)     apply ;;
        flush)     flush ;;
        verify)    verify ;;
        # Self-healing: repair drift only when there is drift, so the steady state never tears
        # down live rules and no in-flight SYN can miss the DNAT during a rebuild window.
        reconcile) verify || { flush; apply; } ;;
        status)
          iptables -t nat -L "$CHAIN" -n -v --line-numbers
          iptables -L "$CHAIN" -n -v --line-numbers
          ;;
        *) echo "usage: ${0##*/} {apply|flush|verify|reconcile|status}" >&2; exit 64 ;;
      esac

  - path: /usr/local/sbin/private-link-healthcheck
    permissions: '0755'
    content: |
      #!/usr/bin/env bash
      # Socket-activated health responder for the Azure Application Health extension.
      #
      # It answers two independent questions, because either failing alone produces a silently
      # broken appliance that a liveness-only probe (Learn's tutorial probes port 22) reports as
      # healthy:
      #
      #   1. Are the forwarding rules actually installed right now?
      #   2. Is at least one configured target actually accepting TCP right now?
      #
      # Note that (2) is a locally originated connection, so it traverses OUTPUT and does not
      # exercise the DNAT rules — which is exactly why (1) is checked separately rather than
      # assumed. Together they cover the full path.
      #
      # No `set -e`: a probe that opens the socket and stalls must produce a response, not an
      # unhandled exit.

      MAP=/etc/private-link-forwarder/forward.map

      # Drain the HTTP request. The content is irrelevant; the timeouts guard against a stalled
      # or half-open probe holding the socket-activated instance open.
      read -r -t 2 _ || true
      while IFS= read -r -t 1 line; do
        [ -z "${line%$'\r'}" ] && break
      done

      state="Healthy"

      /usr/local/sbin/private-link-forwarder verify >/dev/null 2>&1 || state="Unhealthy"

      if [ "$state" = "Healthy" ]; then
        reachable=0
        while read -r listen host port _rest; do
          case "${listen:-}" in ''|\#*) continue ;; esac
          [ -n "${host:-}" ] && [ -n "${port:-}" ] || continue
          if timeout 3 bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/${host}/${port}" 2>/dev/null; then
            reachable=1
            break
          fi
        done < "$MAP"
        [ "$reachable" -eq 1 ] || state="Unhealthy"
      fi

      # Rich Health States contract: always answer 2xx and carry the verdict in the body. A
      # non-2xx is interpreted as "Unknown", which loses the distinction between "the app says
      # it is unhealthy" and "the probe could not reach the app at all".
      body="{\"ApplicationHealthState\":\"${state}\"}"
      printf 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n%s' \
        "${#body}" "$body"

  - path: /etc/systemd/system/private-link-forwarder.service
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      [Unit]
      Description=Private Link forwarding appliance rules
      Documentation=https://github.com/AzureGovGuy/arm-pls-appliance
      Wants=network-online.target
      After=network-online.target systemd-sysctl.service
      [Service]
      Type=oneshot
      RemainAfterExit=yes
      ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/private-link-forwarder apply
      ExecReload=/usr/local/sbin/private-link-forwarder apply
      ExecStop=/usr/local/sbin/private-link-forwarder flush
      [Install]
      WantedBy=multi-user.target

  - path: /etc/systemd/system/private-link-forwarder-reconcile.service
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      [Unit]
      Description=Reconcile Private Link forwarding appliance rules
      After=private-link-forwarder.service
      [Service]
      Type=oneshot
      ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/private-link-forwarder reconcile

  - path: /etc/systemd/system/private-link-forwarder-reconcile.timer
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      [Unit]
      Description=Periodic drift check for Private Link forwarding rules
      [Timer]
      OnBootSec=2min
      OnUnitActiveSec=5min
      AccuracySec=30s
      [Install]
      WantedBy=timers.target

  - path: /etc/systemd/system/private-link-health.socket
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      [Unit]
      Description=Private Link forwarding appliance health endpoint
      [Socket]
      # Loopback only. The Application Health extension runs on the instance and probes locally,
      # so this endpoint never needs to be reachable from the VNet and never needs an NSG rule.
      ListenStream=127.0.0.1:__HEALTH_PORT__
      Accept=yes
      [Install]
      WantedBy=sockets.target

  - path: /etc/systemd/system/private-link-health@.service
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      [Unit]
      Description=Private Link forwarding appliance health responder
      [Service]
      Type=simple
      ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/private-link-healthcheck
      StandardInput=socket
      StandardOutput=socket
      StandardError=journal
      TimeoutStartSec=15s

runcmd:
  - [modprobe, nf_conntrack]
  - [sysctl, --system]
  - [systemctl, daemon-reload]
  - [systemctl, enable, --now, private-link-forwarder.service]
  - [systemctl, enable, --now, private-link-forwarder-reconcile.timer]
  - [systemctl, enable, --now, private-link-health.socket]

final_message: 'Private Link forwarding appliance ready after $UPTIME seconds.'
